source_references.full_readback:
Put \(v=\log x,\ e_\psi(v)=\psi(e^v)e^{-v}-1,\ H=3\cdot10^{12},\ H_* =3000175332800\). B0 is the complete common original-paper foundation, including OpenAIQRH Theorem 1.1 (PDF p. 4) and Platt–Trudgian FiniteRH Theorem 1 (PDF p. 2). Put \(b_0=7/8\). B1 adds exactly FOLLOWUP-D02, with \(b_1=27/32\). Bounds below include nonintegers. Functions counting primes and prime powers take their right-hand values.

## Using FOLLOWUP-D02 before its numerical threshold

For \({\rm Re}\,s>1\), the Euler product and summation by parts give
\[
 -\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)=s/(s-1)+s\int_1^\infty(\psi(t)-t)t^{-s-1}\,dt.
\]
The finite initial integral through \(e^{200}\) is harmless; beyond it the **exact** extra majorant gives locally uniform convergence, also under differentiation, for \({\rm Re}\,s>27/32\). The identity extends there meromorphically (e.g. \(\zeta(s)=s/(s-1)-s\int_1^\infty\{t\}t^{-s-1}dt\) for \({\rm Re}\,s>0\)). Any zero in that half-plane would produce a nonremovable log-derivative pole. Thus \(\beta\le b_1\), including possible equality. This deduction is how the added input strengthens estimates even below \(e^{200}\), not a numerical extrapolation. Its power, not the particular finite coefficient, suffices for this deduction. The exact coefficient and threshold are also used in the direct branch. For real \(0<s<1\) the alternating Dirichlet series \((1-2^{1-s})\zeta(s)\) is positive by grouping pairs; hence no real nontrivial zero was omitted. Nonreal zeros are counted with multiplicity and conjugation symmetry.

source_references.full_readback:
FKS Theorem 3.2 (PDF p. 8) gives the signed Cully-Hugill–Johnston form with admissible parameters \((\log x_M,\alpha,\omega,M)=(40,1/2,0,2.091)\). For real \(x=e^v,\ v\ge61\), use \(T=\sqrt x/6\). It satisfies \(\max(51,\log x)<T<(\sqrt x-2)/5\), and gives a height \(T^*\in[T,2.45T]\) such that
\[
 e_\psi(v)=-\sum_{|\gamma|\le T^*}\exp((\rho-1)v)/\rho+r(v),
 \qquad |r(v)|\le 12.546\,v e^{-v/2}<3v^2e^{-v/2}. \tag{1}
\]
The upper height is below \(\sqrt x\). PT 1809.03134v2 Lemma 2 (PDF p. 4) says \(\sum_{0<\gamma\le t}1/\gamma\le (\log(t/(2\pi)))^2/(4\pi)+0.9321\) for \(t\ge2\pi e\). Thus the two-sided reciprocal mass through \(T^*\) is at most \(.04v^2+2\), and through \(H\) it is less than 117 (certificate.py). All zeros through \(H\) are on \(\beta=1/2\). Equation (1) is only used **pointwise**, with no differentiation or integration of its variable cutoff. In particular it avoids relying on the error-marked Dudek truncation proof discussed in FKS Remark 3.3. The signed integral is proved separately.

source_references.full_readback:
Use FKS Corollary 2.9, (2.17), and Table 8 (PDF pp. 7–8, 26) **at original-paper trust**. For \(3/4\le s\le7/8,\ t\ge H\), the table gives \(N(s,t)\le12t^{8(1-s)/3}(\log t)^{5-2s}+5(\log t)^2\) by rounding upwards. This is reuse of the stated corollary, not regeneration of its optimized table. There is an apparent notation/hypothesis discrepancy: Theorem 2.7 says \(\delta\ge1\) while the table labels a parameter \(\delta\) near .31. We do not use this table as an *independently* proved density result. The fallback below is independent of it.

With \(h=\log H,\ \alpha=(8s-5)/3,\ q=5-2s\), put
\[
 Z(s)=24h^q e^{-\alpha h}/(\alpha-q/h)+10(h^2+2h+2)/H .
\]
Partial summation bounds \(\sum_{\beta>s,|\gamma|>H}1/|\gamma|\) by \(Z(s)\), since \((h+t)^q\le h^q e^{qt/h}\), the denominator is positive, and the second density integral is elementary. If the count uses \(\beta\ge s\) it still bounds this sum. This estimate does not add fictitious off-line mass at \(H\).

Take the grid \(s_0=3/4\), \(3/4+j/2000<b\), the additional point \(27/32\) if \(b=b_0\), and last point \(s_m=b\). Write \(d=1-b\). Layering the high-zero weights gives
\[
 L_b(v)=(.04v^2+2)e^{-v/4}+(3v^2+117)e^{-v/2}
 +\sum_{j<m}Z(s_j)\big(e^{-(1-s_{j+1})v}-e^{-(1-s_j)v}\big).
 \tag{2}
\]
A zero above \(s_0\) is covered up to the next grid point; one exactly at a grid point is covered through that point. The base layer covers all high zeros and the second term covers low zeros and the remainder. Thus \(|e_\psi(v)|\le L_b(v)\). Put \(E_b(v)=L_b(v)+Z(s_0)e^{-v/4}\): the sum in this positive version is \(\sum_{j<m}(Z(s_j)-Z(s_{j+1}))e^{-(1-s_{j+1})v}\), with \(Z(s_m)=0\) **only in that sum**. Coefficient positivity is checked on both grids (and also follows from monotonicity of the displayed \(Z\)). The grids coincide below \(b_1\), so \(L_{b_1}(v)<L_{b_0}(v)\) on their entire common domain.

Dusart Cor. 4.5 (PDF p. 13) gives \(0\le\psi(x)-\theta(x)<(1+1.47\cdot10^{-7})\sqrt x+1.78x^{1/3}\). For \(v\ge24\) the relative cost is at most \(2e^{-v/2}\). Let \(E_b^\theta=E_b+2e^{-v/2}\) (certificate.py: ts). For any \(a\ge160\), \(e^{dv}E_b^\theta(v)\) decreases termwise; write \(C_b(a)=e^{da}E_b^\theta(a)\). This is an entire-ray bound. Refining the *zero-level* grid is harmless; no finite sample of x-values proves a ray.

source_references.full_readback:
Let \(h=\log H,\ \alpha=(8s-5)/3,\ q=5-2s\). In each original FKS Table 8 row use the same upward-rounded \((c,f)\) as refine.py. In the Stieltjes integral of common.md replace the exponential majorant of \((h+w)^q\) by its degree-four Taylor polynomial at \(w=0\), valid for **all** \(w\ge0\) since \(3<q<4\) and the fifth derivative is negative. This gives the two-sided reciprocal-mass allowance
\[
 Z_4(s)=\frac{2c\,h^qe^{-\alpha h}}{\alpha}
       \sum_{k=0}^4\frac{q(q-1)\cdots(q-k+1)}{(\alpha h)^k}
      +\frac{2f(h^2+2h+2)}H
\]
(empty falling product 1). Here \(\int_0^\infty w^k e^{-\alpha w}dw=k!/\alpha^{k+1}\) cancels the Taylor denominators. It is nonincreasing inside each row since each factor decreases there and is positive (\(h>1\)); take the prefix minimum as in common.md, preserving nonincrease across row edges. The degree-four polynomial is bounded by \(h^q e^{qw/h}\), so this sharpens the per-row allowances and the resulting pointwise positive endpoint envelope. The shared \(1/4000\) grid, including \(27/32\), and telescoping construction are unchanged; the positive form also retains the \((.04v^2+2)e^{-v/4}\) bulk term. Use the original \(12.546v e^{-v/2}\) remainder of (1) and \(119e^{-v/2}\) for low zeros plus prime powers. Thus the new θ and corresponding ψ majorants are valid for all \(v\ge61\). Do not infer independent validity of the optimized Table 8 parameter calculation: (2.17) is used as the **stated** corollary, with the printed \(\delta\) discrepancy still documented in common.md. The off-line strip boundary changes from \(7/8\) to \(27/32\) exactly by the Mellin argument of common.md; the new table gains below \(L=200\) are not from the literal D02 inequality at those points.

source_references.full_readback:
For \(k(v)=1\) or \(v^{-1}+v^{-2}\), a signed tail bound valid for \(L\ge39\) is
\[
 \left|\int_L^\infty k(v)e_\psi(v)\,dv\right|
 \le k(L)\left[6e^{-L/2}+(400/H)e^{-dL}\right]\le k(L)B_d(L),
 \quad B_d(L)=[4+6(L^2+4L+8)]e^{-L/2}+(400/H)e^{-dL}. \tag{4}
\]
The larger \(B_d\) is deliberately retained in the table certificates. This result does not use the density corollary and does not assume a regular cutoff in (1).

**Proof of (4).** For \(F(s)=-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)\), integrate the elementary Perron kernel:
\[
 \int_1^x \psi(t)t^{-2}dt
 =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}\frac{F(s)x^{s-1}}{s(s-1)}\,ds .
\]
The scalar kernel applied to \(x/n\) gives \(n^{-1}(1-n/x)\) if \(n\le x\), zero otherwise, by closing to the left or right; at equality the continuous kernel is zero. Absolute convergence on 2 justifies the interchange. By functional-equation reflection (also used in FKS (3.10)), every zero has \(\beta\ge1-b\ge1/8\). Shift to \({\rm Re}\,s=1/10\), crossing the double pole at 1 and the nontrivial zeros only. CH2 Prop. B.8, (B.8) (PDF pp. 46–47) with \(\sigma_+=2,\ a=1\) and the zero count in FKS Lemma 2.1 and Remark 2.2 justify horizontal limits: choose heights in \([N,N+1]\) at distance \(\gg1/\log N\) from all ordinates there or within 1 of that interval, possible by the \(O(\log N)\) count. Then \(F\) is \(O(\log^2 N)\) across the strip at these heights, and the horizontal integrals vanish. Citing (B.8) here requires no finite RH at the chosen heights.

Here are ample explicit vertical bounds for the remainder. For \(|t|\le1000\), subtract CH2 (B.9) at \(s=.1+it\) and \(2+it\). For \(|\gamma|\le2000\) use at most 20000 zeros by PT Lemma 2, each reciprocal difference bounded by \(40+1\) from the horizontal separations. For \(|\gamma|>2000\) the difference is \(\le8/\gamma^2\). The digamma difference costs less than 2 by its convergent partial-fraction difference on \({\rm Re}\,z\ge1\) (or the Euler product for \(\Gamma\)); the pole difference costs less than 3, and \(|F(2+it)|\le\sum_{n\ge2}\log n/n^2<3\). Thus \(|F(.1+it)|<10^6\) there. For \(|t|\ge1000\), (B.8) yields \(|F(.1+it)|<1000\log |t|\): the nearby count is \(<20\log|t|\) by FKS Lemma 2.1 and its Rosser constants in Remark 2.2, each denominator costs at most 40, and the remaining explicit terms with \(\sigma=.1,\sigma_+=2,\ a=1\) are \(<20\log|t|\). Integrate \(1/|s(s-1)|\le 100/9\) for \(|t|\le1\) and \(\le1/t^2\) elsewhere. The resulting vertical integral is \(<5\cdot10^6 e^{-.9L}\).

The residue at 1 is \(L-1-\gamma\), by the Laurent expansion (the constant term of \(\zeta\) is Euler's constant by summation of the defining series against the integral). Each zero contributes \(-e^{(\rho-1)L}/(\rho(\rho-1))\), with multiplicity. For \(0<\gamma<100\) FKS Cor. 2.3 Table 1 (PDF p. 5) gives reciprocal sum \(<.593\), so the square sum there is \(<.593^2\). For \(t\ge100\), \(A(t)=\sum_{0<\gamma\le t}1/\gamma\le(\log t)^2/12+1\) by PT Lemma 2. Partial summation bounds \(\sum_{\gamma\ge Y}1/\gamma^2\) by \(((\log Y)^2+2\log Y+2)/(12Y)+1/Y\) for \(Y\ge100\). The total positive-ordinate square sum including the low zeros is \(<1\); twice its tail above \(H\) is \(<200/H\). Thus the residue sum is absolutely convergent and tends to zero at infinity. Subtract its limit from the formula to get
\[
 \left|\int_L^\infty e_\psi(v)dv\right|
 \le 2e^{-L/2}+(200/H)e^{-dL}+5\cdot10^6 e^{-.9L}
 \le 3e^{-L/2}+(200/H)e^{-dL}.
\]
For decreasing \(k\), integrate by parts against this primitive and use the same decreasing upper majorant inside the integral: the endpoint and the integral together cost at most twice that majorant times \(k(L)\). This proves (4), including the stronger displayed version. The bound on the vertical remainder by one further \(e^{-L/2}\) actually holds for all \(L\ge39\), by \(5\cdot10^6 e^{-.4\cdot39}<1\) (upgrade.py); the explicit formula (1) still only needs to be used on its original domain, in particular for convergence at infinity.

def bound_at(b,v):
        d=1-b
        P=pure_c(b,v)
        mass=(4+6*(v*v+4*v+8))*e(-(F(1,2)-d)*v)+I(F(400,H))
        powers=4*e(-(F(1,2)-d)*v)+10*e(-(F(2,3)-d)*v)
        zz=P+(1+1/v)*mass+powers
        return zz/(1-zz*e(-d*v)/v)

def short_m(a,z,eta):
    # CH2 psi (or literal finite RH), sharper signed primitive, and G.
    # All L>=39; endpoints l,r below are exact rationals.
    a,z,eta=map(F,(a,z,eta))
    assert a>=39 and (5*10**6*e(-F(2,5)*39)).lt(1)
    opts=[]
    for T in (10**7,10**8,10**9,10**10,10**11,10**12,T0):
        assert I(max(T,10**9)).lt(e(F(39)))
        pairs=ch_terms(T)

source_references.full_readback:
Put \(v=\log x,\ e_\psi(v)=\psi(e^v)e^{-v}-1,\ H=3\cdot10^{12},\ H_* =3000175332800\). B0 is the complete common original-paper foundation, including OpenAIQRH Theorem 1.1 (PDF p. 4) and Platt–Trudgian FiniteRH Theorem 1 (PDF p. 2). Put \(b_0=7/8\). B1 adds exactly FOLLOWUP-D02, with \(b_1=27/32\). Bounds below include nonintegers. Functions counting primes and prime powers take their right-hand values.

## Using FOLLOWUP-D02 before its numerical threshold

For \({\rm Re}\,s>1\), the Euler product and summation by parts give
\[
 -\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)=s/(s-1)+s\int_1^\infty(\psi(t)-t)t^{-s-1}\,dt.
\]
The finite initial integral through \(e^{200}\) is harmless; beyond it the **exact** extra majorant gives locally uniform convergence, also under differentiation, for \({\rm Re}\,s>27/32\). The identity extends there meromorphically (e.g. \(\zeta(s)=s/(s-1)-s\int_1^\infty\{t\}t^{-s-1}dt\) for \({\rm Re}\,s>0\)). Any zero in that half-plane would produce a nonremovable log-derivative pole. Thus \(\beta\le b_1\), including possible equality. This deduction is how the added input strengthens estimates even below \(e^{200}\), not a numerical extrapolation. Its power, not the particular finite coefficient, suffices for this deduction. The exact coefficient and threshold are also used in the direct branch. For real \(0<s<1\) the alternating Dirichlet series \((1-2^{1-s})\zeta(s)\) is positive by grouping pairs; hence no real nontrivial zero was omitted. Nonreal zeros are counted with multiplicity and conjugation symmetry.

source_references.full_readback:
Use FKS Corollary 2.9, (2.17), and Table 8 (PDF pp. 7–8, 26) **at original-paper trust**. For \(3/4\le s\le7/8,\ t\ge H\), the table gives \(N(s,t)\le12t^{8(1-s)/3}(\log t)^{5-2s}+5(\log t)^2\) by rounding upwards. This is reuse of the stated corollary, not regeneration of its optimized table. There is an apparent notation/hypothesis discrepancy: Theorem 2.7 says \(\delta\ge1\) while the table labels a parameter \(\delta\) near .31. We do not use this table as an *independently* proved density result. The fallback below is independent of it.

With \(h=\log H,\ \alpha=(8s-5)/3,\ q=5-2s\), put
\[
 Z(s)=24h^q e^{-\alpha h}/(\alpha-q/h)+10(h^2+2h+2)/H .
\]
Partial summation bounds \(\sum_{\beta>s,|\gamma|>H}1/|\gamma|\) by \(Z(s)\), since \((h+t)^q\le h^q e^{qt/h}\), the denominator is positive, and the second density integral is elementary. If the count uses \(\beta\ge s\) it still bounds this sum. This estimate does not add fictitious off-line mass at \(H\).

Take the grid \(s_0=3/4\), \(3/4+j/2000<b\), the additional point \(27/32\) if \(b=b_0\), and last point \(s_m=b\). Write \(d=1-b\). Layering the high-zero weights gives
\[
 L_b(v)=(.04v^2+2)e^{-v/4}+(3v^2+117)e^{-v/2}
 +\sum_{j<m}Z(s_j)\big(e^{-(1-s_{j+1})v}-e^{-(1-s_j)v}\big).
 \tag{2}
\]
A zero above \(s_0\) is covered up to the next grid point; one exactly at a grid point is covered through that point. The base layer covers all high zeros and the second term covers low zeros and the remainder. Thus \(|e_\psi(v)|\le L_b(v)\). Put \(E_b(v)=L_b(v)+Z(s_0)e^{-v/4}\): the sum in this positive version is \(\sum_{j<m}(Z(s_j)-Z(s_{j+1}))e^{-(1-s_{j+1})v}\), with \(Z(s_m)=0\) **only in that sum**. Coefficient positivity is checked on both grids (and also follows from monotonicity of the displayed \(Z\)). The grids coincide below \(b_1\), so \(L_{b_1}(v)<L_{b_0}(v)\) on their entire common domain.

Dusart Cor. 4.5 (PDF p. 13) gives \(0\le\psi(x)-\theta(x)<(1+1.47\cdot10^{-7})\sqrt x+1.78x^{1/3}\). For \(v\ge24\) the relative cost is at most \(2e^{-v/2}\). Let \(E_b^\theta=E_b+2e^{-v/2}\) (certificate.py: ts). For any \(a\ge160\), \(e^{dv}E_b^\theta(v)\) decreases termwise; write \(C_b(a)=e^{da}E_b^\theta(a)\). This is an entire-ray bound. Refining the *zero-level* grid is harmless; no finite sample of x-values proves a ray.

This gives the two-sided reciprocal-mass allowance
\[
 Z_4(s)=\frac{2c\,h^qe^{-\alpha h}}{\alpha}
       \sum_{k=0}^4\frac{q(q-1)\cdots(q-k+1)}{(\alpha h)^k}
      +\frac{2f(h^2+2h+2)}H
\]
(empty falling product 1). Here \(\int_0^\infty w^k e^{-\alpha w}dw=k!/\alpha^{k+1}\) cancels the Taylor denominators. It is nonincreasing inside each row since each factor decreases there and is positive (\(h>1\)); take the prefix minimum as in common.md, preserving nonincrease across row edges. The degree-four polynomial is bounded by \(h^q e^{qw/h}\), so this sharpens the per-row allowances and the resulting pointwise positive endpoint envelope. The shared \(1/4000\) grid, including \(27/32\), and telescoping construction are unchanged; the positive form also retains the \((.04v^2+2)e^{-v/4}\) bulk term. source_references.full_readback:
For \(k(v)=1\) or \(v^{-1}+v^{-2}\), a signed tail bound valid for \(L\ge39\) is
\[
 \left|\int_L^\infty k(v)e_\psi(v)\,dv\right|
 \le k(L)\left[6e^{-L/2}+(400/H)e^{-dL}\right]\le k(L)B_d(L),
 \quad B_d(L)=[4+6(L^2+4L+8)]e^{-L/2}+(400/H)e^{-dL}. \tag{4}
\]
The larger \(B_d\) is deliberately retained in the table certificates. This result does not use the density corollary and does not assume a regular cutoff in (1).

**Proof of (4).** For \(F(s)=-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s)\), integrate the elementary Perron kernel:
\[
 \int_1^x \psi(t)t^{-2}dt
 =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}\frac{F(s)x^{s-1}}{s(s-1)}\,ds .
\]
The scalar kernel applied to \(x/n\) gives \(n^{-1}(1-n/x)\) if \(n\le x\), zero otherwise, by closing to the left or right; at equality the continuous kernel is zero. Absolute convergence on 2 justifies the interchange. By functional-equation reflection (also used in FKS (3.10)), every zero has \(\beta\ge1-b\ge1/8\). Shift to \({\rm Re}\,s=1/10\), crossing the double pole at 1 and the nontrivial zeros only. CH2 Prop. B.8, (B.8) (PDF pp. 46–47) with \(\sigma_+=2,\ a=1\) and the zero count in FKS Lemma 2.1 and Remark 2.2 justify horizontal limits: choose heights in \([N,N+1]\) at distance \(\gg1/\log N\) from all ordinates there or within 1 of that interval, possible by the \(O(\log N)\) count. Then \(F\) is \(O(\log^2 N)\) across the strip at these heights, and the horizontal integrals vanish. Citing (B.8) here requires no finite RH at the chosen heights.

For \(|\gamma|>2000\) the difference is \(\le8/\gamma^2\). The digamma difference costs less than 2 by its convergent partial-fraction difference on \({\rm Re}\,z\ge1\) (or the Euler product for \(\Gamma\)); the pole difference costs less than 3, and \(|F(2+it)|\le\sum_{n\ge2}\log n/n^2<3\). Partial summation bounds \(\sum_{\gamma\ge Y}1/\gamma^2\) by \(((\log Y)^2+2\log Y+2)/(12Y)+1/Y\) for \(Y\ge100\). \[

source_references.full_readback:
Write \(U(v),V(v)\) for upper/lower absolute π allowances (use \(U=0\) on the signed interval). On the domains checked, \(P^+(L)\le1.03/L,\ U(L)<0.01/L\). The first follows by checking at 37 and decreasing terms; for the second, the CH2 branch at \(T=2\cdot10^8\) already gives the bound at 37, and \(v\) times this allowance decreases for \(v\ge37\) apart from a constant, by (6). The tail allowances themselves easily satisfy the same inequality at the tested anchors and decrease after multiplication by \(v\); the certificate's linear loss bound can equivalently be applied to the minimum of that CH2 branch and the tail allowance. Thus normalized loss from the Li proxy is at most
\[
 L^5\left[V(L-1)+2.07\,U(L)\right].
\]
For a lower bound on the proxy itself, expand \(P(L-1)/L\) by the binomial series in \(1/L\) through exponent 26 (all dropped terms positive), and subtract \((P^+(L))^2\). Multiply by \(L^6\). Call the unscaled polynomial coefficients \(D_n\). For \(2\le n\le26\) the coefficient formula above applies; \(c_2,\ldots,c_5=0,\ c_6=1\). For \(N=j+7\), the excess above \(F_j\), multiplied by \(L^{j+1}\), is at least
\[
 D_N+\sum_{n>N}\min(0,D_n)a^{N-n}\qquad(L\ge a).
\]
For finite cells use positive terms too, at their right endpoints, and negative terms at their left endpoints. This derives the certificate's exact slack tests; it is not a numerical evaluation of the true gap followed by extrapolation.

On an entire tail \(L\ge a\), multiplying the error by \(L^{j+1}\) produces nonnegative terms decreasing if \((j+6)/a+1/(a-1)<1/8\). This follows by logarithmic differentiation of (6), since all density tail rates are \(\ge1/8\), the maximum positive power at \(L-1\) is 1, and reciprocal factors only help. The same suffices for (3) of common.md and for the direct D02 transfer. Hence each positive slack test **at the onset** proves its whole tail. For earlier intervals use (6), and the direct finite bounds, all decreasing on their cells; evaluate the normalized positive powers at the right endpoint and all upper-error multipliers at the left. Choose only branches available throughout a cell, in particular split at \(39.3,43,44,58,59\) (the split at 44 is the shifted cutoff). The finite tests cover \([42.8,60]\) for \(F_0\), then \([60,280]\) by CH2 alone, and \([280,\infty)\) with the no-density QRH bound. The finite \(F_1\) checks cover B0 \([47.5,170]\), then refine.py joins \([170,190]\) to its refined B0 tail. For this join it uses (6) with the refined θ majorant at 61 and the global CH2 allowance, taking the minimum. B1 retains that ray. The earlier constant-margin tests overlap the \(F_0\) ray. All finite cells are certified ranges, not sample points.

source_references.full_readback:
Write \(n=38358837682\), \(p_*=14111427770\). The exact counts are \(\pi(n)=1644673232,\ \pi(p_*)=632207037\). On \([n,n+1)\), \(\lfloor x\rfloor=n,\ \lfloor x/e\rfloor=p_*\). The unique root \(r\) there of
\[
 e\,r\,632207037/\log r=(1644673232)^2
\]
lies strictly between \(n+0.2179263651\) and \(n+0.2179263652\). Indeed this left side increases, and endpoint.py verifies both local signs, the floors, and \(R(n)<0\). Therefore \(R(x)\le0\) on \([n,r]\), with equality only at \(r\) there. In particular the literal wording “all \(n<x\le\exp(58)\)” in PT 1809.03134v2 Thm. 2 (PDF p. 3) cannot be used as a true real statement. Neither that literal real theorem nor its proof is needed for the large finite join. Use Dudek–Platt's expressly reported *integer* last failure up to \(10^{11}\) (PDF p. 8, §3.1 first paragraph) and the integer portion of their reported computation through \(1.15\cdot10^{16}\) (Table 1, Lemma 3.4, PDF pp. 9–10). These are at inherited finite-computation trust; the computation in Lemma 3.4 is not conditional on full RH, despite its placement in the RH section. In particular do not use their full-RH analytic continuation of that finite result. For each covered integer \(k>n\), \(R\) is nondecreasing from \(k\) to \(k+1\) with the latter excluded: \(\pi(x)=\pi(k)\) and \(\pi(x/e)\) and \(ex/\log x\) are nondecreasing. This gives the real join \([n+1,1.15\cdot10^{16}]\). Our signed π, finite-height, and CH2 bounds give \(R>0\) already on \(36.95\le L\le37.2\) (checks.py, which also checks \(36.95<\log(1.15\cdot10^{16})\)), and the quantitative rays complete the proof. The largest real failure is \(r\), while \(n\) is the largest integer failure. Strict sign holds on \((r,\infty)\), not at \(r\). A rational closed onset is \(n+0.2179263652\). This locally verified repair addresses the integer-vs-real wording; it does not rerun the original large finite prime computation.

The local count algorithm starts with \(S(v)=v-1\) for every distinct \(v=\lfloor n/i\rfloor\) (separately for each count). Sieve primes in increasing order through \(\sqrt n\), recognizing each \(p\) by \(S(p)>S(p-1)\). The surviving set contains smaller primes and integers not divisible by any smaller prime. For \(v\ge p^2\) exactly \(S(\lfloor v/p\rfloor)-S(p-1)\) current survivors have smallest prime factor \(p\) and are composite; remove them. Process \(v\) in decreasing order, so the smaller index has its old value. Quotient indices are closed under nested division, and all integers through \(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\) occur. Finally only primes remain. All comparisons of the analytic root are via outward arithmetic, not an approximate root finder.

def primepi(n):
    r=isqrt(n)
    V=[n//i for i in range(1,r+1)]
    V+=list(range(V[-1]-1,0,-1))
    S={v:v-1 for v in V}
    for p in range(2,r+1):
        if S[p]==S[p-1]: continue
        base=S[p-1]
        for v in V:
            if v<p*p: break
            S[v]-=S[v//p]-base
    return S[n]
if __name__=='__main__':
    from intervals import I, exp, log, F
    n=38358837682
    E=exp(1)
    K=14111427770
    assert I(K).lt(n/E) and ((n+1)/E).lt(K+1)
    A,B=primepi(K),primepi(n)
    assert (A,B)==(632207037,1644673232)
    def R(t):return E*t*A/log(t)-B**2
    lo=F(n)+F('.2179263651'); hi=F(n)+F('.2179263652')
    assert R(lo).lt(0) and I(0).lt(R(hi)) and R(n).lt(0)
    print(A,B,str(lo),str(hi),R(lo).pt(),R(hi).pt(),R(n).pt())

As in Dusart Thms. 5.6–5.7 (PDF pp. 17–19),
\[

def main():
    g=100000

    ll=log(N);eps=F(1,5)/ll**2
    z=sum((-1)**j*factorial(j)/ll**j for j in range(8))/(2*N*ll)

    es=3*eps/(2*N*ll)
    hs=z+I(-F(es.h,B),F((es+rr+3/(N*N*ll)).h,B))
    ew=3*eps/N
    ws=I(F(1,N))-I(0,F(ew.h,B))+I(0,F((ew+F(6,N*N)).h,B))
    s=q=w=M=K=I(0)
    prev={}
    ends=[912559,2278379]
    plist=primes(N)

    assert [p for p in plist if 2278379<=p<=2278383]==[2278379]
    for p in plist:

        s+=F(1,p);w+=l/p;q+=F(1,p)+h;M+=h;K+=l/(p*(p-1))
        if p in ends:prev[p]=(s,w,q)
    M=gamma-M-hs;K=gamma+K+ws
    print('constants',gamma.pt(),M.pt(),K.pt())

        d=q-gamma-log(l)

\[

 C_s=\sum_{p^m>x,m\ge2}1/(mp^m),\quad

\]
Then \(W=u(L)+C_w,\ S=z(L)+C_s,\ \Delta=z(L)+C_Q\). The tail caps are \(0\le C_w\le G(L)=4e^{-L/2}+10e^{-2L/3}\), and \(0\le C_Q\le C_s\le G(L)/L\). For \(m=2\) use \(\theta(y)\le2y\) (Dusart Thm. 4.2, table PDF p. 11) in partial summation from \(\sqrt{x}\). For \(m\ge3\), on \(p>x^{1/3}\) the full geometric series is at most \(2/p^3\) and integration gives \(6x^{-2/3}\). On \(p\le x^{1/3}\) the first allowed power term is \(<1/x\), the series is at most \(2/x\), and \(\theta(x^{1/3})\le2x^{1/3}\). Divide termwise by \(\log(p^m)>L\) for the other caps. Partial summation, anchoring at infinity, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 u(L)&=e_\psi(L)-\int_L^\infty e_\psi(v)\,dv,\\
 z(L)&=e_\psi(L)/L-\int_L^\infty e_\psi(v)(1/v+1/v^2)\,dv,\\
 z(L)&=u(L)/L-\int_L^\infty u(v)/v^2\,dv .
\end{aligned}\tag{7}
\]
Indeed both centered errors tend to zero by the corresponding Dusart prime-sum limits and the power-tail estimates, and the displayed integrals converge with the ψ estimates. All jumps are included at the right, hence these equalities hold also at integers and prime powers. Alternatively use \(e_\theta(v)=e^{-v}\theta(e^v)-1\) in the first two equations to obtain \(W,S\), and then \(\Delta=S-\sum_{p>x,m\ge2}1/(mp^m)\). The latter subtracted term is at most \(4e^{-L}/L\): use \(\sum_{m\ge2}1/(mp^m)\le1/p^2\) and the θ bound. The exact callbacks to Dusart here are for constants/limits, not their error sizes in the new late result.

def short_m(a,z,eta):
    # CH2 psi (or literal finite RH), sharper signed primitive, and G.
    # All L>=39; endpoints l,r below are exact rationals.
    a,z,eta=map(F,(a,z,eta))
    assert a>=39 and (5*10**6*e(-F(2,5)*39)).lt(1)
    opts=[]
    for T in (10**7,10**8,10**9,10**10,10**11,10**12,T0):
        assert I(max(T,10**9)).lt(e(F(39)))
        pairs=ch_terms(T)
        opts.append((pairs[0][0],pairs[1][0]-2))
    opts.append((A,114))

def primes(N):
    a=bytearray(b"\1")*(N+1);a[:2]=b"\0\0"
    for p in range(2,isqrt(N)+1):
        if a[p]:a[p*p:N+1:p]=b"\0"*((N-p*p)//p+1)
    return [p for p in range(2,N+1) if a[p]]
def hpart(p):
    if p<1000: return -lf(1-F(1,p))-F(1,p)
    h=sum(F(1,j*p**j) for j in (2,3,4))
    return I(h,h+F(2,5*p**5))
def main():
    g=100000
    gamma=sum(I(F(1,k)) for k in range(1,g+1))-log(g)-F(1,2*g)+I(0,F(1,6*g**3)+F(1,12*g**2))
    ll=log(N);eps=F(1,5)/ll**2
    z=sum((-1)**j*factorial(j)/ll**j for j in range(8))/(2*N*ll)
    rr=factorial(8)/(2*N*ll**9)
    es=3*eps/(2*N*ll)
    hs=z+I(-F(es.h,B),F((es+rr+3/(N*N*ll)).h,B))
    ew=3*eps/N
    ws=I(F(1,N))-I(0,F(ew.h,B))+I(0,F((ew+F(6,N*N)).h,B))
    s=q=w=M=K=I(0)
    prev={}
    ends=[912559,2278379]
    plist=primes(N)
    assert [p for p in plist if 912559<=p<=912560]==[912559]
    assert [p for p in plist if 2278379<=p<=2278383]==[2278379]
    for p in plist:
        l=lf(p);h=hpart(p)
        s+=F(1,p);w+=l/p;q+=F(1,p)+h;M+=h;K+=l/(p*(p-1))
        if p in ends:prev[p]=(s,w,q)
    M=gamma-M-hs;K=gamma+K+ws
    print('constants',gamma.pt(),M.pt(),K.pt())
    def test(t,j):
        l=log(t);s,w,q=prev[ends[0] if j==1 else ends[1]]
        if j==0:return (s-M-log(l))*l**3
        if j==1:return (w+K-l)*l**2
        d=q-gamma-log(l)
        return (exp(d)-1 if j==2 else 1-exp(-d))*l**3
    for j,(k,eta) in enumerate([(2278379,F('.2')),(912559,F('.3')),(2278379,F('.2')),(2278379,F('.2'))]):
        end=912560 if j==1 else 2278383 if j==0 else 2278382
        print(j,'at p,join',test(k,j).pt(),test(end,j).pt())
        l=log(end)
        if j==0:err=prev[k][0]-M-log(l)
        elif j==1:err=prev[k][1]+K-l
        else:err=prev[k][2]-gamma-log(l)
        assert I(0).lt(err) and err.lt(F(1,100))
        assert I(eta).lt(test(k,j)) and test(end,j).lt(eta)
        assert I(10).lt(log(k)) and test(k,j).lt(1)
        lo=hi=None

            if I(eta).lt(u):lo=x

        print('crossing bracket',j,str(lo),str(hi),float(lo),float(hi))

def primes(N):
    a=bytearray(b"\1")*(N+1);a[:2]=b"\0\0"
    for p in range(2,isqrt(N)+1):
        if a[p]:a[p*p:N+1:p]=b"\0"*((N-p*p)//p+1)
    return [p for p in range(2,N+1) if a[p]]
def hpart(p):
    if p<1000: return -lf(1-F(1,p))-F(1,p)
    h=sum(F(1,j*p**j) for j in (2,3,4))
    return I(h,h+F(2,5*p**5))
def main():
    g=100000
    gamma=sum(I(F(1,k)) for k in range(1,g+1))-log(g)-F(1,2*g)+I(0,F(1,6*g**3)+F(1,12*g**2))
    ll=log(N);eps=F(1,5)/ll**2
    z=sum((-1)**j*factorial(j)/ll**j for j in range(8))/(2*N*ll)
    rr=factorial(8)/(2*N*ll**9)
    es=3*eps/(2*N*ll)
    hs=z+I(-F(es.h,B),F((es+rr+3/(N*N*ll)).h,B))
    ew=3*eps/N
    ws=I(F(1,N))-I(0,F(ew.h,B))+I(0,F((ew+F(6,N*N)).h,B))
    s=q=w=M=K=I(0)
    prev={}
    ends=[912559,2278379]
    plist=primes(N)
    assert [p for p in plist if 912559<=p<=912560]==[912559]
    assert [p for p in plist if 2278379<=p<=2278383]==[2278379]
    for p in plist:
        l=lf(p);h=hpart(p)
        s+=F(1,p);w+=l/p;q+=F(1,p)+h;M+=h;K+=l/(p*(p-1))
        if p in ends:prev[p]=(s,w,q)
    M=gamma-M-hs;K=gamma+K+ws
    print('constants',gamma.pt(),M.pt(),K.pt())
    def test(t,j):
        l=log(t);s,w,q=prev[ends[0] if j==1 else ends[1]]
        if j==0:return (s-M-log(l))*l**3
        if j==1:return (w+K-l)*l**2
        d=q-gamma-log(l)
        return (exp(d)-1 if j==2 else 1-exp(-d))*l**3
    for j,(k,eta) in enumerate([(2278379,F('.2')),(912559,F('.3')),(2278379,F('.2')),(2278379,F('.2'))]):
        end=912560 if j==1 else 2278383 if j==0 else 2278382
        print(j,'at p,join',test(k,j).pt(),test(end,j).pt())
        l=log(end)
        if j==0:err=prev[k][0]-M-log(l)
        elif j==1:err=prev[k][1]+K-l
        else:err=prev[k][2]-gamma-log(l)
        assert I(0).lt(err) and err.lt(F(1,100))
        assert I(eta).lt(test(k,j)) and test(end,j).lt(eta)
        assert I(10).lt(log(k)) and test(k,j).lt(1)
        lo=hi=None
        for i in range((end-k)*1000+1):
            x=k+F(i,1000)
            u=test(x,j)
            if I(eta).lt(u):lo=x
            if u.lt(eta):hi=x;break
        assert (lo,hi)==tuple(map(F,[('2278382.112','2278382.114'),('912559.997','912559.998'),('2278381.711','2278381.712'),('2278381.575','2278381.576')][j]))
        print('crossing bracket',j,str(lo),str(hi),float(lo),float(hi))
if __name__=='__main__':main()

source_references.full_readback:
small.py uses an exact Eratosthenes sieve through \(N=8\cdot10^6\) and directed arithmetic for the cumulative sums and constants. For \(\gamma\), the trapezoid sum for \(1/t\) gives
\(0\le\gamma-(H_g-\log g-1/(2g))\le 1/(6g^3)+1/(12g^2)\) at \(g=10^5\); each trapezoid error is at most \(\sup|f''|/12\). For the constants, use \(|\theta(t)-t|\le\epsilon t\) for \(t\ge N\) with \(\epsilon=.2/\log^2N\), from Dusart Thm. 4.2 (table PDF p. 11; surrounding argument pp. 11–12). The tail for \(B_3\) has main term \(1/N\) from \(p^{-2}\), error at most \(3\epsilon/N\) from partial summation, and higher powers nonnegative at most \(6/N^2\) by \(\theta(t)\le2t\). For \(M\)'s subtracted tail use the weight \(g(t)=1/(2t^2\log t)\): its integral is \(\frac12\int_{\log N}^\infty e^{-v}/v\,dv\); θ uncertainty is at most \(3\epsilon/(2N\log N)\) by partial summation. Eight integrations by parts bracket this integral with the alternating factorial expansion and the first omitted term. Higher powers in \(M\)'s tail add at most \(3/(N^2\log N)\) by the same θ control. Finite evaluation of \(\sum_{m\ge2}1/(mp^m)\) keeps terms 2–4 for \(p\ge1000\) and bounds the tail by \(2/(5p^5)\); for smaller primes it uses the exact log identity. These bounds justify both constants and local signs. Failure at any point arbitrarily close below each root proves minimality for that coefficient on a final real ray, regardless of additional hypotheses.

## Whole-domain envelopes and what the comparisons mean

The following specifies simultaneous numerical envelopes for all real \(x\ge2\), including where none of the displayed simple late inequalities is yet available. Infima are of **valid bound values**, not of observations. They can be evaluated using convergent elementary integrals, or enclosed by finite integration followed by the explicit power tails. Intersect intervals, and keep direct relative-product controls on their given scale.

* For relative ψ take the minimum of applicable: CH2 Cor. 1.2 (all permissible \(T\)), 1.3 and 9.3; FiniteRH Cor. 1; Dusart Prop. 3.2 Table 1 (PDF pp. 8–9) and Thm. 3.3; FKS Cor. 1.4, Thms. 1.1–1.2 formula families (4.1), (5.2) at their legitimate parameters, and their tabulated controls (Tables 5–6, pp. 22–23); PT 1809.03134v2 Thm. 1 Table 1; (2) and (3) of common.md. The source-row numbers needed for straightforward evaluation are in source_rows.json, generated from the bound originals. Use the original hypotheses at row endpoints (where \(x_0>e^{1000}\) is required there is no need to admit the row with exponent exactly 1000). At \(x=2\) do not use the open FKS Cor. 1.4 domain. B1 keeps the B0 branches and adds both B1 variants and the literal D02 majorant on \(L\ge200\).
* For θ take the ψ bound plus the prime-power bound (common.md), and the minima with Dusart Thm. 4.2 (all rows), FiniteRH Cor. 1, and PT 1809.03134v2 Cor. 1 (all rows). For shifted intervals one can intersect the symmetric bound with the interval obtained by subtracting a number in \([0,(\psi-\theta)_{\rm cap}/x]\) from the ψ interval. The same pointwise θ input is available to the Ramanujan envelope.
* For \(u\), take the CH2 weighted bounds and (7): keep the best endpoint ψ bound, use the minimum of integrated absolute envelope and the applicable signed bound (4). For \(z\), similarly use both formulas (7), allowing the best \(u\) envelope in the last integral, not only one original \(T\). Keep the θ-based alternatives for \(W,S\). Add the positive power-tail intervals to \(u,z\) as appropriate, and use \(\Delta=S-\sum_{p>x,m\ge2}1/(mp^m)\) as an additional log control. From any logarithmic interval \([\ell,u]\), the sharp transformed envelope from that interval alone is \(\max(|e^\ell-1|,|e^u-1|)\) for \(Q\) and \(\max(|e^{-\ell}-1|,|e^{-u}-1|)\) for \(P\).
* Intersect with all the direct Dusart 5.6–5.9 error bounds (Theorem 5.9 statement is PDF p. 19), the local repairs and all the simple bounds above on their valid domains. The error bounds for \(P,Q\) and the related prime sums are correlated, not independent tests.

This gives whole-domain non-worsening, not a claim that no other argument using B0 can do better. It is substantial to compare against the reconstructed QRH branches, not only the literal Dusart estimates. For example one can prove **strict dominance on the entire ray \(L\ge170\)** against the explicit B0 envelope just specified (using the numerical rows, fixed-height CH2 family and the common reconstruction). Here are lower comparisons for the *bound values*, not for the actual errors:

1. For \(L\ge170\), the B0 endpoint radii for ψ, θ, and the independent CH2 weighted bound are all at least
\[
 q(L)=\min(1.04\cdot10^{-12},.0039e^{-L/8}).
\]
CH2 weighted and ψ have constant floors at least \(\pi/(H_*-1)\); for the centered ψ form the shift is less than \(10^{-6}\) times its radius. The finite RH rays and Cor. 9.3 have expired. For the B0 telescoping density bound use the last six grid increments, all with \(Z\ge Z(.8745)>.011\), so their sum is \(\ge .011(1-e^{-.003L})e^{-L/8}\). The tuned grid works as well: its last twelve increments have \(Z>.0107\), giving \(.0107(1-e^{-.003L})e^{-L/8}\). The no-density bound is larger. The minima with the tabulated rows and elementary powers preserve the lower comparison: source_rows.py checks the left comparisons to \(.0039e^{-L/8}\), and the logarithmic decay rates of each stretched-exponential row and elementary powers are smaller than \(1/8\) throughout each relevant ray. source_references.full_readback:
A better power exponent is not just a matter of sharpening the prime-power correction. If, for some \(d'>5/32\), one proved \(W(x)=O(x^{-d'}(\log x)^k)\), partial summation in \(\sum_p(\log p)p^{-s}\) gives
\[
 \sum_p\frac{\log p}{p^s}=\frac1{s-1}-B_3+(s-1)\int_1^\infty W(x)x^{-s}\,dx
 \quad({\rm Re}\,s>1)
\]
(with the same normalization extended below 2). The last integral continues to \({\rm Re}\,s>1-d'\). Adding the absolutely convergent \(m\ge2\) terms, holomorphic for \({\rm Re}\,s>1/2\), would exclude zeros with \({\rm Re}\,s>\max(1-d',1/2)\). Bounds for \(S\) with the same better exponent imply such a \(W\) bound with one extra \(\log x\), by partial summation with weight \(\log x\); a better relative product exponent first transfers to \(\Delta\), then to \(S\) at a cost \(O(1/(x\log x))\). Thus a power improvement beyond \(5/32\) would need genuinely stronger zero information. This does not preclude better coefficients or logarithmic savings at the same boundary.

Here is the transfer used for the π error. If \(|\theta(e^v)e^{-v}-1|\le\sum_i c_i v^{k_i}e^{-d_iv}=D(v)\) for \(v\ge a\), with \(c_i\ge0,\ k_i\in\{0,1,2\},\ d_i\le1/2\), then
\[
 |\pi(e^v)e^{-v}-f(v)|
 \le e^{a-v}(P_a+D(a)/a)+
 \sum_i c_i v^{k_i-1} e^{-d_iv}\left(1+\frac1{v(1-d_i-2/a)}\right).
 \tag{6}

def transfer(terms,a,v,anchor):
    return anchor*e(a-v)+sum(c*v**(k-1)*e(-d*v)*(1+1/(v*(1-d-F(2,a)))) for c,k,d in terms)
